# Detecting and controlling microbes

> *How does a laboratory find out which microbe is present, and how are unwanted microbes removed? Both
> answers follow from the traits described in the earlier chapters.*

## What each method reads {#sec-det-reads}

A laboratory method does not show "the organism" directly. Each method reads one property, and what it
reads sets what it can and cannot tell you. Keeping this in mind explains most of what seems arbitrary
about diagnostic microbiology.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/method-sorter.yml"></div>

## Seeing: stains and microscopy {#sec-det-microscopy}

Microscopy is fast, cheap and widely available, and it reads structure. The Gram stain, from [*How
bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-envelope), reads the envelope
and sorts most bacteria into two groups within minutes. The acid-fast stain reads a waxy, mycolic-acid
wall, so it finds mycobacteria that the Gram stain misses.

The limits follow from what a stain reads. A stain gives a category, not a species: purple cocci in
chains could be one of several organisms. It also needs enough organisms to be present, typically
around 10⁴ to 10⁵ per millilitre of fluid, so a negative result does not exclude infection.
Organisms with no wall, or too thin to resolve, give nothing useful.

## Growing: culture {#sec-det-culture}

Culture reads growth. Its main advantage over every other method is that it yields a living
isolate, which can then be identified, tested against drugs, and compared with isolates from other
patients during an outbreak investigation. Media are chosen for what they allow to grow or what they
reveal.

| Type of medium | What it does | Example of use |
|---|---|---|
| **Non-selective** | Supports a wide range of organisms | A general plate for a sample from a normally sterile site |
| **Enriched** | Adds nutrients that fastidious organisms cannot make | Chocolate agar, which supplies factors released from lysed red cells |
| **Selective** | Contains agents that suppress unwanted organisms | Isolating one pathogen from a sample full of resident microbiota |
| **Differential** | Makes colonies look different according to a metabolic property | Blood agar, on which haemolysis distinguishes streptococci |

Culture conditions decide what a laboratory can find. An anaerobe will not grow on a plate kept in air,
as in the lab case in [*How bacteria are built and get energy*](bacteria-build-energy.qmd#sec-bact-case).
A slow-growing organism is missed if plates are discarded too early, as in the *Helicobacter* case in
[*The microbial world*](microbial-world.qmd#sec-world-case). An obligate intracellular organism will not
grow on agar at all. In none of these situations does a negative culture mean the sample contained
nothing.

Culture is also slow. Many bacteria need overnight incubation, and mycobacteria can take weeks, which
is the main reason molecular methods have become central.

## Detecting molecules {#sec-det-molecular}

**Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs)**, of which the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is the
best-known example, copy a target sequence many times until it can be detected. They are fast and
highly sensitive, and they can detect organisms that cannot be cultured. Three consequences follow from
what they read:

- They detect sequence, not viability. Dead organisms, or nucleic acid remaining after an infection has
  resolved, can give a positive result, so a positive test does not always mean active infection.
- They detect only their target. A test designed for one organism will not report another, whereas
  culture can grow an organism nobody was looking for.
- Their sensitivity makes contamination a real risk, which is why laboratories separate the work
  done before and after amplification.

**MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry** reads the protein profile of a colony and matches it against a database,
identifying most organisms within minutes once they have grown. It has largely replaced long series of
biochemical tests. **Whole-genome sequencing** reads the entire genome, at a resolution that can show
whether isolates from two patients belong to the same strain, and it is now standard in outbreak
investigation.

## Reading the host: serology {#sec-det-serology}

**Serology** detects the patient's antibodies, so it is evidence about the host's history rather than
about the organism's presence now. Two patterns carry most of the interpretation. IgM appears early and
then falls; IgG appears later and persists, sometimes for life. A rise in antibody level between
**paired sera**, samples taken one to two weeks apart, indicates recent infection.

The usual pitfall follows directly: a single positive IgG result may reflect an infection years ago, or
vaccination. Serology is most useful for organisms that are hard to culture, for infections diagnosed
after the organism has gone, and for assessing immunity.

## Testing drug susceptibility {#sec-det-mic}

Once an organism has been grown, its susceptibility to drugs can be measured. The standard quantity is
the **minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC)**, the lowest concentration of a drug that prevents
visible growth.

<div data-island="mic-reader" data-src="/diagrams/mic-reader.yml"></div>

The laboratory converts the MIC into a category using a **breakpoint**, the concentration agreed to
separate organisms likely to respond from those that are not. Breakpoints are set by committees such as
EUCAST and CLSI and are revised as evidence accumulates, so they are looked up rather than memorised.
Two cautions apply at this stage. A report of "susceptible" describes the organism in a tube, not the
patient: the drug still has to reach the site of infection at an adequate concentration. And a result
is only as good as the sample, which is why samples are ideally taken before treatment starts.

## Controlling microbes {#sec-det-control}

Three terms are used precisely in practice and loosely in conversation. **Sterilisation** kills or
removes all microbial life, including bacterial spores. **Disinfection** removes most organisms from an
inanimate object, but does not reliably kill spores. **Antisepsis** applies the same idea to living
tissue, as in skin preparation before a procedure.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-sterilisation-disinfection.yml"></div>

What survives each method can be predicted from earlier chapters. Bacterial spores survive boiling
and alcohol, so instruments that enter sterile tissue are autoclaved. Enveloped viruses are readily
inactivated by alcohol and detergents, because their lipid envelope is fragile; non-enveloped viruses
are more resistant, which is why hand washing matters in outbreaks of hand, foot and mouth disease.
Prions resist routine sterilisation entirely and need specific, extended protocols.

The same logic applies to hands. An alcohol hand rub is faster and more effective against most
organisms, but when spores are a concern, soap and water are preferred, because washing physically
removes what alcohol does not kill.

## Preventing infection {#sec-det-prevent}

Prevention acts on the links of the chain of infection in [*Transmission, outbreaks and One
Health*](transmission-outbreaks.qmd#sec-trans-chain). Two measures need introducing here.

**Vaccination** makes a host immune without causing disease. Vaccines contain inactivated organisms,
live attenuated organisms, purified components such as proteins or capsular polysaccharides,
**toxoids** (inactivated protein toxins), or nucleic acid encoding an antigen. Two principles recur.
Capsular polysaccharides alone produce a poor response in young children, so they are linked to a
protein in a **conjugate vaccine**, which greatly improved protection against encapsulated bacteria.
And vaccination protects unvaccinated people too, by reducing transmission: the herd immunity effect.
The immunology block covers the mechanisms.

**Antimicrobial stewardship** limits selection for resistance by using antimicrobials only when
indicated, at the right dose and for the right duration. [*How bacteria copy themselves and
change*](bacterial-genetics.qmd#sec-gen-resistance) explains why this is a problem of populations as
much as of individual patients.

## From principles to organisms {#sec-det-close}

Part I has covered how microbes are built, how they obtain energy and change, how they cause damage,
how they spread, and how they are detected and controlled. Part II begins with [*A map of the
bacteria*](../microbes/bacteria-map.qmd), which uses these traits to organise the bacterial groups you
will hear named in lectures.
